title: How the Real Vice City Happened — Minute by Minute
hook: Vice City is Miami. And the real city's history is stranger than any game: a bus crash in Havana, 125,000 people in one summer, a city on fire, and a reporter who counted the dead.
about: The real history behind Grand Theft Auto's Vice City, told from both sides: Julia Tuttle and the Great Freeze, the 368 voters (162 of them Black) who made Miami a city, the 1926 hurricane's deadly eye, Prohibition rum runners and Al Capone on Palm Island, Overtown and I-95, the Cuban exile and the Freedom Flights, the Cocaine Cowboys and Dadeland, Arthur McDuffie and the 1980 riots, Héctor Sanyustiz's bus and the Mariel boatlift, Time's 'Paradise Lost?', the South Florida task force, Scarface, Miami Vice, and how it all became Vice City, from GTA in 1997 to GTA VI.
talkNote: Dialogue scenes are dramatized; every fact comes from the sources below.

beats.say: Wednesday, the eleventh of July, 1979. About half past two in the afternoon. Dadeland Mall, south of Miami, the busiest shopping centre in the city.
A white Ford van rolls slowly across the car park. On its side, painted in neat letters: Happy Time Complete Party Supply.
Inside are two men: a Colombian cocaine trafficker called German Jimenez Panesso, and his bodyguard, Juan Carlos Hernandez. Two gunmen walk in, and open fire with machine guns.
The police call the van a war wagon. One officer gives the killers a nickname the whole country will learn: the Cocaine Cowboys.
Now, if you have ever played a Grand Theft Auto game, this place may feel strangely familiar. Pastel buildings, palm trees, fast boats, neon at night, and money nobody can quite explain.
That's because Vice City, the city in the games, is Miami. It has been there since the very first Grand Theft Auto, in 1997, and the series keeps coming back to it.

scene.date: Liberty City · San Andreas · Vice City

beats.say: So why does a game studio keep coming back to the same city, game after game, for almost thirty years?
In 1980, a bus crash in Havana set off an exodus of a hundred and twenty five thousand people across the sea to it, while its own neighbourhoods burned. A year later, its morgue ran out of room.

And through almost all of it, one woman stood at the edge of the police tape with a notebook. Her name was Edna Buchanan. You have probably never heard of her. She wrote down more than five thousand violent deaths in this city.

scene.date: reported by one Miami Herald reporter

beats.say: This is the real Vice City, from both sides. Minute by minute, and decade by decade.
Fast forward to 1891. A widow from Cleveland, Ohio, Julia Tuttle, moves to the north bank of the Miami River with her two grown children. She owns land. Almost nobody else lives there.
She tells a friend: it is the dream of my life to see this wilderness turned into a prosperous country.

lines: "It is the dream of my life

beats.say: To build a city, she needs a railway. And the man with the railway is Henry Flagler, who has run his Florida East Coast line down to Palm Beach. Not one mile further.

talk.text: Bring the railway south, Mr Flagler.
There's nothing down there, Mrs Tuttle.
There's land. And there will be people.

beats.say: Then the weather helps her. On the twenty fourth and twenty eighth of December 1894, and again on the sixth of February 1895, killing frosts hit Florida.
It works. Flagler sees ruined farmers and a frost free bay, and extends the railway. In April 1896, the first train steams into Miami.
Three months later, on the twenty eighth of July 1896, the men of the settlement meet in a pool hall on the river to vote. To become a city, they need three hundred registered voters.

scene.place: VOTERS NEEDED TO MAKE A CITY

talk.text: Then let's make it a city.

beats.say: Three hundred and sixty eight men. And here is the part that usually gets left out: a hundred and sixty two of them were Black, many from the Bahamas. Without them, there would have been no city of Miami that day.

scene.place: THE BLACK VOTERS WHO MADE MIAMI A CITY

beats.say: And the city they made pushed them aside at once. Black residents were allowed to live in only a few places. The main one was just north west of downtown. It was called Colored Town. Later, it would be called Overtown.
Thirty years later, Miami is the fastest growing city in the United States. The nineteen twenties land boom has arrived, and everybody wants a piece of paradise.
By 1926, the boom is already running out of buyers. And on the eleventh of September, ships far out in the Atlantic report a hurricane.
Just after midnight, the storm arrives. A category four hurricane, gusts up to about a hundred and fifty miles an hour, roaring across Miami Beach and over the bay.
Then, around dawn, it stops. The wind dies. The rain stops. For about thirty five minutes, it is completely calm.

Most of the people in Miami are newcomers from the boom. They have never been through a hurricane. They think it's over. They walk out into the streets to look at the damage. Some go to the beach to look at the waves.

talk.text: That's not the end. That's the eye.

beats.say: They are standing in the eye of the storm. The second half hits from the opposite direction, harder than the first. Most of the people who die in Miami that day are killed after the calm.
Remember that hurricane. Fifty five years later, a famous magazine will use it to describe what happens to Miami next.
Meanwhile, the United States has banned alcohol. Prohibition. And Miami has a gift for smugglers: the Bahamas, British islands where drinking is legal, are a short boat ride away.
And in 1928, the most famous bootlegger in America moves in. Al Capone, the boss of Chicago, buys a house on Palm Island, a man made island dug from the bottom of Biscayne Bay.
He pays forty thousand dollars, in cash. And he buys it from Clarence Busch, of the beer brewing Busch family. A brewer selling his house to the king of illegal beer. You couldn't make it up.
Now go back to Colored Town, the district the city's Black founders were pushed into. Over the next fifty years, something remarkable grows there.

talk.text: The Lyric. You should have heard her.

beats.say: Then, in the nineteen sixties, the government decides to build an interstate highway into downtown Miami. Interstate 95, and a link road to the beaches, Interstate 395.

talk.text: Where are we supposed to go?

beats.say: More than twelve thousand residents are forced out. Nearly all of them are Black. Most cannot move to white neighbourhoods, so they crowd into poorer districts nearby, like Liberty City.

Remember the expressways, too. In 1980, the space under one of them will shelter the newest arrivals in Miami. And Liberty City, where the people of Overtown were pushed, is where this city will burn.
January 1959. In Cuba, Fidel Castro's revolution takes power. And Miami, a short flight away, is about to change for good.
Before the revolution, about fifty thousand Cuban Americans live in the United States. Right after it, around two hundred thousand Cubans come to South Florida.
Downtown, a tower built in 1925 as the headquarters of the Miami News newspaper becomes the Cuban Assistance Center.

From December 1965 to April 1973, the Freedom Flights carry Cubans from Varadero Beach to Miami, twice a day. In all, about three hundred thousand people. The largest and longest resettlement of Cuban refugees the United States government ever ran.
By the late nineteen seventies, Colombian traffickers are flying and shipping cocaine through South Florida, and fighting each other for control of it, in the open.
Detectives name a suspect: Griselda Blanco, the Colombian trafficker they called the Godmother. She allegedly owed one of the dead men money. She was never tried for Dadeland.
Now meet the hidden person of our story. Edna Buchanan, from Paterson, New Jersey. A police reporter at the Miami Herald since 1973, at a time when women were almost never given the police beat.

talk.text: Everybody's somebody. What was his name?

beats.say: The seventeenth of December 1979, early in the morning. Arthur McDuffie, thirty three, a Black insurance salesman and a former Marine, is riding his black and orange Kawasaki motorcycle in north Miami. His licence is suspended.
Police officers chase him for about eight minutes. When it ends, a group of white officers beat him. He dies four days later, on the twenty first of December.
The officers try to hide what they did. Edna Buchanan and others uncover the lies. Officers are charged with manslaughter, and with tampering with evidence.
The trial is moved to Tampa. It will end in May 1980. And in May 1980, Miami will have more than one thing to deal with.
Havana. Tuesday, the first of April 1980. A young man called Héctor Sanyustiz has been planning something in secret for months.
He and four others get on a city bus, route 79, a British made Leyland. One of them is the driver, a friend in on the plan.

talk.text: Everybody off. The bus is broken.

beats.say: Sanyustiz takes the wheel and floors it towards the embassy of Peru. Cuban guards outside open fire on the bus.

The bus smashes through the fence onto the embassy grounds, Peruvian territory. Sanyustiz is wounded. And one of the guards, Pedro Ortiz Cabrera, is killed, hit by a bullet from the guards' own crossfire.
The Peruvian diplomat in charge, Ernesto Pinto Bazurco, grants the five asylum. Cuba demands them back, to be tried for the guard's death. Peru refuses.

talk.text: They asked for asylum. They have it.
Then you can guard them yourselves.

beats.say: On Good Friday, the fourth of April, Castro pulls every guard away from the Peruvian embassy. The statement from Havana says the embassy will now be solely responsible for whatever happens there.

lines: for what occurs in their embassy."

beats.say: Word spreads through Havana by mouth. And within about forty eight hours, around ten thousand eight hundred people pour into the embassy grounds.

More than ten thousand people cram into the embassy's gardens. From Washington's side, this is proof of how many Cubans want out. From Castro's side, the people in that garden are criminals, bums and anti socials, and he wants the world to know it.

scene.header: How the Cuban government described them, 1980

talk.text: Peru? Are they taking us to Peru?

beats.say: Then Castro surprises everyone. On the twentieth of April, he announces that anybody who wants to leave Cuba can go, through the port of Mariel, west of Havana. As long as someone comes to pick them up.
On the twenty first of April, the first boat from Mariel ties up in Key West, with forty eight people on board. A bus that drove through a fence has just opened a door between two countries.
Within days, Mariel harbour turns into a floating city. Pleasure boats, fishing boats, shrimp boats, hundreds of them, waiting their turn to load.

Between April and October 1980, around one thousand seven hundred boats make the crossing. They carry about one hundred and twenty five thousand Cubans to Florida. Around twenty five thousand Haitians arrive in the same months.

talk.text: Built for twelve. I count sixty.

beats.say: In Key West, the scene is surreal. Holiday makers are water skiing between the refugee boats.

On the fifth of May, President Jimmy Carter speaks to the League of Women Voters. Ours is a country of refugees, he says. We'll continue to provide an open heart and open arms to refugees seeking freedom from communist domination.

lines: We'll continue to provide an open heart
and open arms to refugees seeking freedom

beats.say: Most of the arrivals are claimed by relatives and go to live in Miami. About eighty five thousand of them settle there. The city's Cuban population grows by about a fifth in one summer.
And then the other side of the story comes out. Castro has not only let people go. He has opened his prisons and mental hospitals, and put some of those people on the boats too.

So how many were criminals? More than twenty three thousand arrivals tell immigration officers they have a criminal record in Cuba. But many of those records are for things that are not crimes in the United States at all.

lines: Many for acts that are not crimes

beats.say: In the end, Cuba agrees to take back two thousand seven hundred and forty six of them: people the United States judged to be criminals. That's about two in every hundred arrivals.

scene.place: SENT BACK TO CUBA AS CRIMINALS

beats.say: Now go back to May 1980. The boats are pouring into Key West. And on Saturday the seventeenth of May, in Tampa, the jury in the McDuffie case comes back.
An all white, all male jury. After about three hours of deliberation, it finds the officers not guilty.

talk.text: He's dead. And it was nobody?

beats.say: The news reaches Miami that afternoon. People march from Liberty City towards the Dade County justice building. By that night, Liberty City, Overtown, and other Black neighbourhoods are burning.
For three days there is rioting, arson, looting and sniping. Governor Bob Graham sends in the National Guard. The Guard and the police seal off Liberty City.
At least eighteen people are killed, both Black and white. Property damage is estimated at around a hundred million dollars.

Think about the timing. In the very same month, tens of thousands of new arrivals are landing a few miles away, and Washington is promising them an open heart and open arms. In Liberty City, people who have been here for generations watch that, from behind a police cordon.
In 1981, Dade County settles a civil lawsuit with Arthur McDuffie's family, for one point one million dollars.

lines: Dade County settles the civil lawsuit
filed by the family of Arthur McDuffie:

beats.say: Miami has a riot, a refugee crisis and a cocaine war, all at once. In 1980 the city records five hundred and seventy three murders.
In 1981, six hundred and twenty one. Two years earlier, it was three hundred and forty nine. The number has nearly doubled.
The summer of 1981. The Dade County medical examiner has more bodies than the morgue can hold. So the office rents a refrigerated truck, to keep the overflow cold.
She writes: many of the corpses have had familiar faces. Cops and killers, politicians and prostitutes, doctors and lawyers. Some were my friends.

scene.header: Edna Buchanan, The Corpse Had a Familiar Face
lines: "Many of the corpses have had familiar faces:
cops and killers, politicians and prostitutes,

beats.say: Then, on the twenty third of November 1981, Time magazine puts South Florida on its cover, under two words and a question mark. Paradise Lost?
The story begins: an epidemic of violent crime, a plague of illicit drugs and a tidal wave of refugees have slammed into South Florida with the destructive power of a hurricane.

lines: "An epidemic of violent crime, a plague of illicit drugs
and a tidal wave of refugees have slammed into
South Florida with the destructive power

beats.say: A hurricane. Fifty five years after the storm with the treacherous eye, Miami is in the eye of another one.
On the twenty eighth of January 1982, President Ronald Reagan announces a special task force for South Florida.
The man in charge is the Vice President, George Bush. For really the first time, the military is brought in against the smugglers: military aircraft and ships, alongside the police agencies.

On television, Bush gives the numbers: cocaine seizures up fifty four percent. Then the reporter Geraldo Rivera asks: are you stopping the drugs coming in, or merely diverting them? Bush answers: I think we're doing both.

lines: RIVERA: "Are you stopping the drugs coming in
or are you merely diverting them?"

beats.say: In 1986, Edna Buchanan wins the Pulitzer Prize, for, in the judges' words, her versatile and consistently excellent police beat reporting. The New Yorker profiles her.

talk.text: Then I'd better get back to work.

beats.say: Hollywood has been watching all of this. In 1983, the director Brian De Palma and the writer Oliver Stone remake a 1932 gangster film, Scarface, and move it to Miami.
Their gangster, Tony Montana, played by Al Pacino, is a Cuban refugee who arrives on the Mariel boatlift, and becomes a cocaine kingpin.

The film opens with a written prologue, then a real television clip of Fidel Castro. The prologue says that of the hundred and twenty five thousand refugees who landed in Florida, an estimated twenty five thousand had criminal records.

lines: "Of the 125,000 refugees that landed in Florida,

beats.say: Twenty five thousand. The serious, violent ones American officials actually identified: about two thousand seven hundred.

Miami's Cubans are angry before a single scene is shot. A Miami Herald columnist writes that the film will tell the nation and the world that the prototype of the American gangster of the 1980s was a Mariel refugee.

of the 1980s was a Mariel refugee."

beats.say: The film carries a note at the end: Scarface is a fictional account of the activities of a small group of ruthless criminals. It is released on the ninth of December 1983. Many critics pan it. It becomes the sixteenth highest grossing film of the year anyway.

beats.say: Now meet another man who read the news about Miami. Anthony Yerkovich, a writer on the police drama Hill Street Blues.
He reads in the Wall Street Journal that twenty percent of all the unreported income in the United States comes from Dade County, Florida. A county with half of one percent of the nation's people.

scene.header: Wall Street Journal, as Yerkovich remembered it
lines: 20% of unreported income in the US:

talk.text: Of all the dirty money in America.

beats.say: He writes a pilot about two undercover detectives in Miami. The executive producer, Michael Mann, insists on the title: Miami Vice. And he gives the show one rule for the look: no earth tones.

Miami Vice premieres in September 1984. Pastel suits, sports cars, speedboats, pop songs over the action. Each episode costs about one point three million dollars, one of the most expensive shows on television.

Miami Vice runs until 1989, with twenty Emmy nominations and four wins. And the image it leaves behind, neon, pastel, palm trees and danger, is exactly the image a game studio will reach for, thirteen years later.
1997. A small studio called DMA Design releases a top down crime game called Grand Theft Auto. Three cities: Liberty City, San Andreas, and, for the finale, Vice City.
In 2002 the studio, now Rockstar, goes back to Vice City in full 3D. The year is 1986. The hero, Tommy Vercetti, is voiced by Ray Liotta, the first protagonist in the series who talks.

Everything you've just heard is in there, turned into satire. The neon of Miami Vice. The mansion and the boatlift of Scarface. Pastel hotels, speedboats, a cocaine trade, a city that is beautiful and violent at the same time.
And then, the fourth of December 2023. Rockstar releases the first trailer for Grand Theft Auto Six. Vice City is back, but in the present day, in a state called Leonida.
From the pool hall vote in 1896 to the year the game is set, 1986: ninety years. The ninety years that made Vice City.

From one side, Vice City is a joke about Miami. Neon, gangsters, chaos. From the other side, Miami is full of people who lived through the real thing: Cubans who crossed the sea, families from Overtown, cops, refugees, reporters.

The game has neon. The real city has names. Pedro Ortiz Cabrera, the guard who died at the embassy fence. Arthur McDuffie. The thousands Edna Buchanan wrote about, one by one, so that every one of them was somebody.
Julia Tuttle wanted to see this wilderness turned into a prosperous country. She got her wish. It just came with everything else.

lines: "It is the dream of my life

beats.say: So next time you drive down Ocean Drive in Vice City, under the neon, remember the real one. It's a lot stranger, and a lot more human, than any game.
